taxonomyNote: NatureServe (Burbrink 2000, 2001) splits the former P. obsoletus complex into P. obsoletus (Western Ratsnake), P. alleghaniensis and P. spiloides, and lists P. obsoletus as Western Ratsnake; 'gray rat snake' is the batch's common name, and Animal Diversity Web's page title for P. obsoletus is 'Eastern Rat Snake' while its text says western rat snake.
fieldMarks: Glossy black dorsal scales often speckled with brown, orange or yellow; creamy white belly; distinct checkerboard pattern.
Slender body with a rounded head and weakly keeled scales; adult snout-vent length 96-154 cm, males larger; one of the longest snakes in North America.
Juveniles grayish with tan blotches, darkening with age.
behavior: Diurnal especially in cool spring, more active at night in summer; partly arboreal and climbs to raid tree-hollow nests; swims.
Adults eat mainly mammals (66% in one study), plus birds and eggs, lizards, other snakes and amphibians.
When cornered coils, opens mouth and may vibrate the tail against leaves like a rattlesnake; brumates October-February in hollow trees, burrows, caves or stumps.
habitat: Rocky hillsides and canyons, scrub fields, prairie farmland, deciduous forest, swamps, woodland edges, grasslands and rural structures.
range: Central United States, north to southern Minnesota, south along the Mississippi River to the Gulf Coast; west to southern Nebraska and the eastern halves of Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas. Not in Canada.

lookalikes.name: Central (eastern) ratsnake
lookalikes.howToTell: Western ratsnake has a distinct checkerboard pattern; both have weakly keeled scales (Animal Diversity Web).
